Breaking the ice: The Ice Hotel

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South African designer Corban Warrington recreates a steam train out of snow at the mythical Ice Hotel in Sweden

Unique Selling Point:
Corban Warrington is only the second African in 35 years to be showcased at the mythical Ice Hotel - a boutique hotel that pops up out of nothing once a year in the Swedish lapland.

Summary:
Corban Warrington, a South African designer, is only the second African in 35 years to design a room for the world-renowned Ice Hotel. His design, Yesterday’s Tomorrow, brings South African heritage to life in the heart of the Arctic, transforming blocks of ice into a visual paradox of culture and art - prestigious milestone in any designer's career.

Key Themes:
Visual Paradoxes:
- The Ice Hotel’s construction site of chaos, turned into a palace of ice
and snow.
- Corban’s design of a steam train, sculpted from ice, inspired by the
Elgin railway market brings to life steam - the antithesis of the freezing cold
– in an ice sculpture
- How culture and artistic expression bloom in the frozen Arctic winter
where so much struggles to survive

The Mythical Torne River:
- The Ice Hotel is built with ice blocks cut from this river, which melt back
into it each year - "From which the ice hotel comes, it will eventually return."

Artistic and Environmental Impact:
- Focus on the hotel’s artistic energy, environmental consciousness, and
impact on local communities.
- Sustainability of the project in the face of changing climatic conditions
and the snow arriving late each year.

Further information:
Visual Approach:
- Piece to be compiled with visuals shot by on-site videography team over
3 days and 2 night, complimented by archive footage and b-roll provided by
Ice Hotel PR team. From 4-6 December on site in Jukkasjäarvi, Sweden.
- Visual narrative to be driven dynamic fast-moving, walk-and-talk and in
situ interviews alongside scenic wide shots, drone footage and go-pro
shots capturing the grandeur and detailed process of constructing the Ice
Hotel within its immediate environment
- Focus on the strong visual contrasts of an environment dominated by ice
and darkness coming alive with the explosion of artistic expression and
intricate lighting.

Swedish media liaison Steffan Pearson @ 9375 sek for the 3 days

Press Release:


The Ice Hotel: A frozen masterpiece

In the heart of Sweden’s Lapland, a mythical wonder emerges each European winter: the world-renowned Ice Hotel. Sculpted from blocks of pristine ice and snow, this boutique hotel is an architectural marvel that exists only temporarily, melting away each spring before its spectacular rebirth in the frosty embrace of winter.

Each year, designers from around the globe submit proposals for a chance to transform one of its rooms into a work of art. Last December, South African designer Corban Warrington achieved a rare honor, becoming only the second African in 35 years to contribute to this iconic project. His design, "Yesterday’s Tomorrow", seamlessly fuses South African heritage with Arctic aesthetics, crafting a spectacular piece of art in a paradoxical union of steam and ice.

Carte Blanche joined Corban in the Arctic as he turned his ambitious vision into a tangible masterpiece, wielding picks and shovels to breathe life into his design. This remarkable journey highlights not only his talent but also the power of art to bridge worlds, cultures and climates.

Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

Script:


INTRO PTC
Here in the frozen forests of Lapland in northern Sweden, nestled along the banks of the mythical Torne River, an extraordinary piece of art takes shape every European winter. A magical frozen palace crafted from ice and snow from this very frozen river. Destined to melt back into it every single summer. Welcome to the Ice Hotel.
VO: Two hundred kilometres north of the Arctic Circle lies Jukkasjärvi, an ancient Sami village, famed as a meeting place for people from near and far.
LUCA RONCORONI: “Hi Nickolaus, Welcome!”
NICKOLAUS BAUER: “Luca, Thanks for having us!”
LUCA RONCORONI: “As you can see this is still a building site, so we need to kit you up with safety gear. SO we can all see where you are and then you have a nice matching helmet.”
NICKOLAUS BAUER: “Nice! Yellow is my favourite colour!
LUCA RONCORONI: “Let me show you this is the ceremony hall of the ice hotel.”
VO: Luca Roncoroni is Ice Hotel’s Creative Director.
LUCA RONCORONI: We have a floral theme for this year and on all these benches we will have Reindeer fur.”
VO: Ice Hotel opened in 1989 after founder Yngve Bergqvist hosted an art exhibition in a hall made of ice. Some guests spent the night in the gallery and a dream was born.
INTERVIEW BYTE: LUCA RONCORONI, Ice Hotel Creative Director
“We borrow frozen water from the river just behind our shoulders. And we build- sleeping rooms, entrances, furniture - everything. 35 years ago and here we are in a place where 70,000 people from all over the world come and visit every year.”
VO: 5000 tonnes of ice is harvested from the frozen river every winter and for the first time a South African designer is part of the process.
UPS Corban gopro
VO: Cape Town engineer, Corban Warrington and his right-hand-man, Dan Afonso swapped sunny South Africa for this ice-challenge in early December last year.


INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
Anyone from around the world – doesn’t matter who you are, what you do – anyone can submit a design for an ice hotel suite and if they like your concept you have the opportunity to come here.


VO: 20 ice rooms and 15 art suites are designed and built every year by a carefully selected team. Competition to design a suite is intense with hundreds of applications annually.


INTERVIEW BYTE: LUCA RONCORONI, Ice Hotel Creative Director
“90 percent never make it here. What we are looking for is new and fresh ideas and a person that has a bit more of a drive of shaping, creating things and see their vision from the paper, from the sketch grow up and be what our guests will experience.
VO: For Corban, it was sixth time lucky.
INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
“***I got that email and i was just like, nah… No, no. They made spelling error, something went wrong along the way. I’m like, i think they got the wrong guy. But actually, they dig the concept And they offered me the opportunity to come and bring the vision to life.”
VO: Corban’s design – yesterday’s tomorrow of a Steam Train, a tribute to early 20th century Art Deco
INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
“What would our cities, our cars and trains look like had that movement continued?”
VO: Designing a room made of ice is one thing. Physically building it in a few weeks, in a foreign medium, is a whole other challenge!
INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
“I’ve never even built a snowman before so I am completely in the dark. But actually we have so quickly found rhythm and we’ve completely fallen in love with working with snow and ice. “
LINK PTC
You think you’ve prepared for this but it’s even colder than it looks. I’m wearing just about every layer of clothing I brought with me… And I’m desperate for more. South Africans were not built for this cold…
VO: 4-hours of daylight take some getting used to. And only 15 days to complete the hotel means work carries on late into the night…
Once only known for its centuries old iron ore mine, the ice Hotel has spawned a flourishing tourism industry here…
INTERVIEW BYTE:


NICKOLAUS: That is so good! How long have you been mushing?


INTERVIEW BYTE: STEPHANIE PELUCHON, Husky Voice
“16 years now. I came as a guest first - worked as a volunteer and now I have my own operation of 19 dogs - who wouldn’t want to work with these guys!.”


VO: There are more dogs than people in Jukkasjärvi. And these Siberian Huskies can trek for up to 200kms a day. They aren’t the only animals around this year.


INTERVIEW BYTE: ANNASOFIA MÅÅG, Swedish Designer of “Oops wrong room!”
“They are a very tragic sign of what human kind can do wrong - where they can go wrong I think.”


NICKOLAUS: “And you know Rhinos are very very special in South Africa?
ANNASOFIA: “***I haven’t seen one in real life - yet I am making one in snow! That’s strange! But it is a dream for me to see it for real!
VO: You blink and it's night again. But darkness brings the celestial dance of the northern lights
UPS INTERVIEW BYTE STAFFAN WALLNER, Lapland guide
“It looks like a shower that moves towards you, like a colourful hole that wants to absorb you.”
VO: Steffan Wallner is a local guide.
INTERVIEW BYTE STAFFAN WALLNER, Lapland guide
“There are many different folklores - some believe you are in limbo between life and death if you died an early or tragic death and those are your relatives up there. You should pay respect and not tease the northern lights because then you can make the higher powers angry.”
VO: Under the watchful eye of the ancestors, the hotel too is adorned with lights. Lead lighting technician, Charlotte Tentau.
INTERVIEW BYTE: CHARLOTTE TENTAU, Ice Hotel lead light technician
“You don’t want to see that there is light, you just want to experience it.
“It's really hard to plan for lighting in ice and snow because the ice will decide for you what you can do or not. An ice block can look really different - one ice block from another. “
INTERVIEW BYTE: LUCA RONCORONI, Ice Hotel Creative Director
“It's deforming all the time, every piece of ice you pick up from the river, the freezing process is different. So you have different veins, different cracks, different bubbles. So every ice piece will react in a different way when you sculpt it and even more when you put light on it. You need to be super super flexible. You cannot come here with a drawing to the millimeter***”
VO: This unpredictability meant a few hiccups for Corban and Dan.
INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
“We’ve been dreading this part of building up snow half way up - two and half meters up on the wall and shaping it to look like actual steam. And it was just absolute hell - we just couldn't get it right - it kept falling off. It's such a challenge trying to do justice to a hot element in a frozen form. *** We took a whole new approach on it where we started finding snice - its a combination of snow and ice. Massive blocks and we have been chainsawing and hand chiseling them.”
NICKOLAUS: This is paradox though as you are creating the very antithesis of steam out of Ice and Snow?
CORBAN: “It's so trippy that in reality this thing is 200 degrees celsius when its alive and moving, when shaping it its minus 15 outside and I’m working shaving a piece of ice while shivering my butt off”
VO: To survive and thrive in these conditions - you need to embrace the cold!
LINK PTC
“This is a local custom that has existed for hundreds of years.”
LINK PTC
“The health benefits of an ice plunge and Sauna are many ranging from improving your circulation or increasing your pain threshold. But right now I’m just focusing on survival. Here we go…THAT IS SO INTENSE! THAT IS SO INTENSE!”
LINK PTC
“Like the rest of this environment, that was brutal but beautiful in its own unique way - I am happy I did it!”
VO: After weeks of frozen sweat and toil… Ice Hotel 35 opened on the 13th of December…
Nickolaus: CHEERS!
Corban: CHEERS!
Nickolaus: That was hectic!
Corban: That WAS hectic!
Nickolaus: How do you feel now that you’re done now?
INTERVIEW BYTE: CORBAN WARRINGTON, South African designer
“The whole of the trip has been surreal. Literally from the start to finish - from the landscape to the environment to this incredible place and what they have achieved here. And to say that I am a part of that - it's literally surreal”
Nickolaus: To the ice hotel
Corban: To the ice hotel!!
VO: For the next 4 months visitors can book any one of these spectacular suites for a cool R15- to R25,000 per night…
By late spring it all melts away … and the process starts again.
VISUALS:
BOAT COVERED IN SNOW ON THE FROZEN RIVER




*****

END
